name: LoRA / QLoRA tail-query rewriter
est_cost_usd: 4 GPU-h x R(A100 80GB $/GPU-hr, from the cloud pricing page); worked example at an illustrative $3/GPU-hr = $12. Hours basis: playbook §11 Cost and effort: "One 8B QLoRA run is hours on a single A100/H100-class GPU"
expected_result: Expect a LoRA adapter to be a viable delivery vehicle for this task rather than full fine-tuning, and expect the run to finish in hours on one A100/H100-class GPU. Expect the G3 gate to need BOTH a task metric and a general-capability regression suite, because LoRA's published trade-off is that it "learns less and forgets less" than full fine-tuning.
citation: LoRA, Hu et al., arXiv:2106.09685 (2021). QLoRA, Dettmers et al., NeurIPS 2023, arXiv:2305.14314. "LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less", TMLR 2024, arXiv:2405.09673. Prior deployment of a Llama-3-8B LoRA tail rewriter at Instacart is recorded in the playbook (§11, Maturity and evidence). No number in this README is a measurement of a production retailer's model.

name: DPO preference tuning of the Sparky rewriter
est_cost_usd: 3 GPU-h x R(A100 80GB $/GPU-hr, from the cloud pricing page); worked example at an illustrative $3/GPU-hr = $9. Hours basis: playbook §12 Cost and effort: "M. Training is cheap (LoRA). Preference data and judge calibration are the effort."
expected_result: Expect DPO to move tone/format/preference behaviour, and expect it NOT to fix factual errors - the playbook and the DPO literature both route factual correctness to retrieval or to a verifier (technique 13). Expect the dominant failure mode to be length exploitation, which is why the harness reports pairs dropped by the length guard. The playbook's own acceptance criterion - win rate >=55% against the SFT model with a 95% CI lower bound above 50% - is a **target to be measured**, not a result.
citation: DPO, Rafailov et al., NeurIPS 2023, arXiv:2305.18290. SimPO, NeurIPS 2024, arXiv:2405.14734. The >=55% win-rate figure is the playbook's §12 AC1 target and is explicitly marked as a proposal there.

name: RLVR with a programmatic verifier (GRPO)
gpu_sku: 2x NVIDIA H100 80GB - one rollout (vLLM) + one trainer (Azure Standard_NC80adis_H100_v5 / GCP a3-highgpu-2g)
est_cost_usd: 24 GPU-h x R(H100 80GB $/GPU-hr, from the cloud pricing page); worked example at an illustrative $6/GPU-hr = $144. Hours basis: playbook §13 Cost and effort: "L. Rollout GPU plus trainer plus verifier engineering." 2 GPUs x 12 h
expected_result: Expect RLVR to sharpen a capability the SFT model already has - schema validity, unit normalisation, evidence grounding - rather than to add knowledge; that is the consistent finding in the RLVR literature and the reason the playbook warns against "expecting new knowledge from RL". Expect the binding constraint to be verifier quality: a weak verifier is rewarded by degenerate outputs, which is why `verifier.py` carries an F1 term and an evidence -grounding term and asserts that the honest answer outscores every hack in its self-test. Expect a human reward-hacking audit before G3. The playbook's "schema-valid rate from ~96% to over 99.5%" is marked `[PROPOSAL target]` there and is not claimed here.
citation: GRPO in DeepSeekMath, arXiv:2402.03300. DeepSeek-R1, arXiv:2501.12948 (Nature 2025). DAPO, arXiv:2503.14476. On the limits: "Does RL really incentivise reasoning beyond the base model?", arXiv:2504.13837.

name: On-policy distillation (GKD, reverse KL)
gpu_sku: 2x NVIDIA H100 80GB - teacher scoring pool + student trainer (Azure Standard_NC80adis_H100_v5 / GCP a3-highgpu-2g)
est_cost_usd: 20 GPU-h x R(H100 80GB $/GPU-hr, from the cloud pricing page); worked example at an illustrative $6/GPU-hr = $120. Hours basis: playbook §14 Cost and effort: "M-L. Cheaper than RL per point of quality, but needs a teacher scoring pool." 2 GPUs x 10 h
expected_result: Expect on-policy distillation to beat offline distillation on the student's own error distribution, because offline training never shows the student the states it actually reaches - this is the exposure-bias argument the GKD paper makes. Expect the economics, not the quality, to decide the run: §14 US-14.2 requires a break-even calculation (`breakeven_requests = training_cost / (teacher_cost_per_req - student_cost_per_req)`) attached to the request, and the script prints that contract with no numbers filled in, because they are FinOps inputs.
citation: GKD / on-policy distillation, Agarwal et al., ICLR 2024, arXiv:2306.13649. Thinking Machines Lab, "On-Policy Distillation", Oct 2025 (vendor blog). A large US retailer's existing 7B->BERT-base offline distillation on 170M pairs is recorded in the playbook (§14, Maturity and evidence).

name: FP4 (NVFP4) continued pre-training spike
gpu_sku: 8x NVIDIA B200 (Blackwell, native NVFP4). Azure ND B200 v6 / GCP A4 [VERIFY region + quota; lead times are the real constraint]
est_cost_usd: 48 GPU-h x R(B200 (Blackwell) $/GPU-hr, from the cloud pricing page); worked example at an illustrative $10/GPU-hr = $480. Hours basis: playbook §15 retailer example: a 1B-token continued-pre-training spike. 8 GPUs x 6 h. Doubles because the FP8 control run is mandatory
expected_result: Expect this to be a **feasibility spike whose likely outcome is "defer"**, not a deliverable. The only large-scale evidence today is vendor-reported at 12B scale, the recipes are version-sensitive, optimizer states stay FP32/BF16 so the run is not 4-bit end to end, and the playbook places FP4 in the Assess ring and explicitly outside 90-day scope. Expect the decision criterion to be a loss curve within ~1% of the FP8 control at equal tokens AND a downstream eval delta inside the CI - loss alone is not sufficient. Expect FP4 to bring **no** benefit to techniques 11-14; QLoRA's NF4 is a storage quantisation and a different thing.
citation: NVIDIA, "Pretraining LLMs with NVFP4", arXiv:2509.25149 - a 12B model trained on 10T tokens tracking the FP8 baseline; vendor-reported. TetraJet-v2, arXiv:2510.27527. FP8 as the mainstream default: DeepSeek-V3, arXiv:2412.19437. The +-1% loss-gap criterion is the playbook's §15 AC1 acceptance criterion, not an observed result.

name: Research replication agent
gpu_sku: 1x NVIDIA L4 (GCP g2-standard-8) / 1x A10 (Azure Standard_NV36ads_A10_v5) in a T1 sandbox with egress limited to a package mirror
est_cost_usd: 8 GPU-h x R(L4 / A10 $/GPU-hr, from the cloud pricing page); worked example at an illustrative $1/GPU-hr = $8. Hours basis: task_spec.yaml budget.wall_clock_h = 8, gpu {type: L4, count: 1}; usd_hard_cap 150 is the binding cap
expected_result: Expect a scaffold, not a replication. The strongest published evidence is that 2025 frontier agents reached a 21.0% replication score on PaperBench, below the ML PhD baseline, with the characteristic failure being a plausible method description attached to a codebase that does not run correctly. Expect most runs to land under the playbook's 0.5 engineer-handoff threshold. Expect the value to be engineer-hours saved on scaffolding, and expect any agent self-report of "reproduced" to be treated as unverified until the human grader signs it.
citation: PaperBench, Starace et al. (OpenAI), ICML 2025, arXiv:2504.01848 - best agent 21.0% replication score. The rubric hierarchy and the 0.3/0.5 decision thresholds follow the playbook's §17 spec.

name: Serving benchmark harness (shared by 23/24/25)
gpu_sku: none - CPU load-generator client; it runs beside the endpoint under test
est_cost_usd: 0 GPU-h (CPU-only client); the GPU cost belongs to the endpoint it measures
expected_result: Expect the harness to be the single place a serving number is allowed to originate in this project. Expect the structural prefix ratio it reports in `--smoke` (shared prefix tokens / (prefix + query tokens)) to be a **ceiling** on prefix reuse for this prompt layout, never a cache hit rate - the hit rate is only ever read from `vllm:prefix_cache_hits / vllm:prefix_cache_queries`.
citation: vLLM Prometheus metric names checked against vLLM stable docs; the parser is unit-tested in `--smoke` against a recorded exposition string.

name: PagedAttention + automatic prefix caching (vLLM)
gpu_sku: 1x NVIDIA L4 (GCP g2-standard-8) / 1x A10 (Azure Standard_NV36ads_A10_v5) for the 8B FP8 tail-QU rewriter
est_cost_usd: 4 GPU-h x R(L4 / A10 $/GPU-hr, from the cloud pricing page); worked example at an illustrative $1/GPU-hr = $4. Hours basis: playbook §23 Cost and effort: "S. Config + prompt restructuring, 1-2 weeks incl. load tests." 1 GPU x 4 h of load testing
expected_result: Expect large throughput gains over naive serving and a TTFT drop roughly proportional to the share of prompt tokens that are shared prefix - PagedAttention's published result is 2-4x throughput over prior systems at the same latency. Expect the gain to be workload-shaped: it comes from the shared prefix, so it evaporates on unique long documents. Expect prompt-layout regressions, not engine problems, to be the usual cause of a hit-rate drop, which is why the lint rule and a hit-rate alert both exist. The playbook's "prefix hit ~95%, p99 fits 60 ms on L4 FP8" for UC1 is marked `[PROPOSAL, benchmark in PoC]` there and is not claimed here.
citation: vLLM PagedAttention, Kwon et al., SOSP 2023, arXiv:2309.06180 - 2-4x throughput against prior systems. SGLang RadixAttention, NeurIPS 2024, arXiv:2312.07104. Automatic prefix caching is on by default in the vLLM V1 engine.

name: EAGLE-3 speculative decoding (vLLM)
gpu_sku: 8x NVIDIA H100 80GB (Azure Standard_ND96isr_H100_v5 / GCP a3-highgpu-8g); the 70B FP8 target uses TP=4, the draft head TP=1
est_cost_usd: 128 GPU-h x R(H100 80GB $/GPU-hr, from the cloud pricing page); worked example at an illustrative $6/GPU-hr = $768. Hours basis: playbook §24 Cost and effort: "M. 2-4 weeks incl. draft training (few GPU-days) and batch sweeps." draft train 8 GPUs x 12 h = 96, k/batch sweep 8 GPUs x 4 h = 32
expected_result: Expect a meaningful inter-token-latency reduction at low-to-moderate batch and expect the gain to SHRINK as batch rises - published OSS measurements on H100 show 1.81x throughput at batch 2 falling to 1.38x at batch 64. Expect the gain to be sensitive to domain shift, so expect to retrain the draft head after every target fine-tune. Expect output distribution to be unchanged; if greedy outputs differ, something is wrong, not faster. Do not assume any published speedup transfers to production retail traffic - that is exactly what the sweep is for.
citation: EAGLE-3, Li et al., NeurIPS 2025, arXiv:2503.01840. The 1.81x @ batch 2 / 1.38x @ batch 64 figures are SGLang project-reported on H100; P-EAGLE's 1.05-1.69x over EAGLE-3 on B200 is vendor/OSS-reported (vLLM blog, 2026-03-13). All are other people's measurements on other workloads.

name: Prefill/decode disaggregation + KV tiering
gpu_sku: 2x 8-GPU H100 80GB nodes with RDMA (Azure ND96isr_H100_v5 InfiniBand / GCP a3-highgpu-8g GPUDirect-RDMA): 1 prefill pool + 1 decode pool
est_cost_usd: 128 GPU-h x R(H100 80GB $/GPU-hr, from the cloud pricing page); worked example at an illustrative $6/GPU-hr = $768. Hours basis: playbook §25 Cost and effort: "L. 8-12 weeks incl. RDMA capacity, tuning and failure-mode testing." a replayed-peak load-test campaign of 16 GPUs x 8 h
expected_result: Expect roughly 1.5-2x goodput under SLOs **for long-prompt workloads**, and expect a net loss on short prompts - the split only pays when prefill genuinely stalls decode. Expect the adoption gate to be the playbook's own AC1: >=1.5x goodput against an aggregated baseline at the same TTFT/ITL SLOs on replayed peak traffic, or do not adopt. Expect the real constraints to be RDMA SKU availability and quota lead time, plus the ops complexity of pinning llm-d/Dynamo/vLLM versions together. Expect a privacy review: the remote KV tier can hold state derived from shopper text and needs encryption plus a retention TTL.
citation: DistServe, OSDI 2024, arXiv:2401.09670. Mooncake, FAST 2025, arXiv:2407.00079. LMCache, arXiv:2510.09665. The ~1.5-2x goodput range for long-prompt workloads is the playbook's §25 summary of that literature; the >=1.5x adoption gate is the playbook's §25 AC1 target.
